title: In-Place Tokenizer Expansion for Pre-trained LLMs
hook: On-device models ship small vocabularies to save memory, so languages added later get shredded into extra tokens. This recipe grows the tokenizer after the fact — no retraining from scratch.
key_points: Tokenizers are fixed at pretraining time and sized to the corpus of that era; languages prioritized later get split into far more tokens per word, raising latency and energy cost.
Recipe: continue the existing tokenizer's BPE merges on a multilingual corpus so old tokens carry over unchanged, and initialize new token embeddings as the mean of their source sub-token embeddings.
Two-stage adaptation (embedding-only training, then full-model continued pretraining) recovers the original checkpoint's quality.

Applied to LFM2-8B-A1B (an 8B MoE model) to produce LFM2.5-8B-A1B with a 128K tokenizer: Hindi and Vietnamese now use ~2.4-2.6x fewer tokens (up to 4x for Thai), for an estimated 2.2-3.7x per-character decode speedup.
content_html: Vocabulary choices made at pretraining time stick around for the life of a model. If a language gets added to the priority list later, it still gets chopped into many more tokens per word than languages the original tokenizer was built for — which costs latency, compute, and energy every time someone uses the model in that language. This paper proposes a way to fix that after the fact, without retraining the tokenizer or the model from zero.
extra_html:
Jimmy T. H. Smith and a team spanning Liquid AI and MIT continue the existing tokenizer's byte-pair-encoding merges on a multilingual corpus, so nearly all the original tokens survive unchanged and every new token decomposes exactly into old sub-tokens. New embedding rows start as the mean of their source sub-token embeddings rather than random noise, and a two-stage process — embedding-only tuning, then a round of full-model continued pretraining — recovers the source checkpoint's quality.

Applied to LFM2-8B-A1B, an 8B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, the recipe produces LFM2.5-8B-A1B with a 128K-token vocabulary. Hindi and Vietnamese text now takes roughly 2.4x and 2.6x fewer tokens to encode (up to 4x for Thai), which the authors translate into an estimated 2.2-3.7x per-character decode speedup on their reference devices. They release both the model weights and the expanded tokenizer, along with notes on approaches that didn't work. Source: arXiv, arxiv.org/abs/2607.15232.

related.title: Subword Tokenization with Byte-Pair Encoding
related.hook: Whole words make a giant vocabulary; single characters make long sequences. Subwords split the difference — and let models read words they've never seen.

related.title: SentencePiece: Language-Independent Tokenization
related.hook: Most tokenizers assume you can split on spaces first. SentencePiece drops that assumption and tokenizes raw text directly — in any language.

flashcards.prompt: Why do on-device models suffer more than cloud models from a small, fixed tokenizer vocabulary?
flashcards.back_html: Embedding and LM-head matrices are a small fraction of a huge cloud model's parameters, but a material share of a compact model's per-token decode cost — so on-device models ship small vocabularies and accept fragmentation for languages outside them.

flashcards.prompt: How does this recipe expand a tokenizer's vocabulary without retraining the tokenizer from scratch?

choices.text: It continues the existing tokenizer's BPE merges on new multilingual data, keeping old tokens unchanged and initializing new embeddings as the mean of their source sub-tokens
It discards the old tokenizer entirely and trains a brand-new one on the multilingual corpus
It randomly initializes all new token embeddings and retrains the full model from random init

flashcards.explanation_html: Because new tokens have an exact decomposition into old source tokens, their embeddings can be seeded sensibly rather than from scratch, which is what makes the two-stage recovery cheap.

flashcards.prompt: What efficiency gain did the expanded 128K tokenizer produce for LFM2.5-8B-A1B on Hindi and Vietnamese?
flashcards.back_html: Roughly 2.4x and 2.6x fewer tokens per input respectively (up to 4x for Thai), translating into an estimated 2.2-3.7x per-character decode speedup on the reference devices.
